I now have the direct source K70d91: shell caps bistability threshold; indentation provides a continuous route for near-threshold geometries; thinner shells → asymmetrical buckling before snap-through, more robust to snap-through. That's highly relevant to my "same geometry can be snap-bistable or continuously reversible" idea — a published precedent: near-threshold geometry gives continuous route. So my "吸附式双稳 vs 连续可逆" is partially named (continuous transition route near threshold), though not via static-length traversal of a unilateral stop device.

K8c87c (method): equilibrium manifold + continuation; saddle-node bifurcation position can be tailored; intermediate rotation input in the sequence matters (path-dependent energy accumulation). This is genuinely transferable: to my device, the "release surface" is a saddle-node of the constrained equilibrium manifold, and sequence/path matters.

K413da (method): analytical snap-through for arbitrary initial shape beams; two solutions depending on axial force level; bifurcation and bistability conditions, snapping force equations; superposition of initial shape and buckling modes. Transferable: for a beam/rotor with initial shape (installation offset), the bistability condition is a relation between initial shape amplitude and axial force level; explicit expressions. This suggests a concrete representation for my device: treat rotor+spring as a beam with initial shape; "bistable vs monostable" transition at a critical ratio of initial-shape amplitude to axial load. Hmm, careful with actual content: I only have the abstract. It says two kinds of solutions depending on axial force level; bistability conditions derived. For a V-shape inclined beam, snap-through occurs.

Now the key learning task: the gap I asked was about (a) unilateral-constraint hysteresis category vs energy barrier; (b) static-length traversal switching between adsorption bistability and continuous reversibility; (c) RPM under state coarse-graining.

What the controller returned: no direct source for "unilateral stop hysteresis as a category" (all irrelevant), one direct for bistability/monostability threshold + continuous transition route near threshold, two methods for snap-through thresholds (continuation/saddle-node; analytical bifurcation conditions). So: the literature retrieves everything through the energy-landscape/snap-through frame; my "constraint activation" framing is NOT found as a named category — but that's not evidence it's new (retrieval failure). More usefully: the constraint-generated barrier physics appears in the hydrogel paper (K3b9128): "bending to the opposite side is hampered by the geometric constrain ... elastic energy accumulated until threshold" — i.e., the geometric constraint flips the sign of the resisting energy as a function of configuration, so constraint and barrier are not alternatives. This is the crucial conceptual move: constraint and energy barrier are two descriptions of the same object when the constraint is a *two-sided/reversible* clamp; my device's stop may be one-sided (the constraint can be lost, not just hit).

Key substantive learning: the constrained-buckle papers distinguish (i) geometric constraint that *sets where* the equilibrium can be vs (ii) energy storage that must be overcome. In the S-shaped gel, two buckles share a middle constraint, and the neighbor's state changes the cost of the same state ("If the two units buckle to the same direction, the connection region will have a very high elastic energy") — that's mechanically exactly the "w" and "b" mechanisms: neighbor state changes the energy of the connection, hence shifts the effective thresholds. And "collective snapping ... one part snaps, the other follows without external drive" — that's an avalanche/latch across a shared constraint, i.e., my "same-γ double flip" but produced by energy minimization under a shared constraint rather than by a force-moment field. Importantly: it shows that a shared constraint node produces *opposite-direction* coupling (anti-ferromagnetic-like): neighbor snapping upward causes the other to snap opposite direction to minimize total energy. That's a mechanism for b>0! In my device, pair_B is b>0 (anti-ferro) — the "crossed geometry" pair. So a concrete mechanism: b>0 arises when two rotors share a constraint (pivot/common mount) so the low-energy combination is anti-aligned. Whereas pair_A b<0 (ferro) would correspond to... rotors connected so same direction lowers energy (e.g., parallel springs, shared support that simply shifts).

That's a genuinely useful development: my hypothesis coupling_torque_moments says b and 1−w come from the same coupling torque function; the gel-buckle paper gives an explicit physical mechanism for the *sign structure* being set by the topology of the shared constraint (parallel vs serial/S-shaped connection). This adds a conceptual relation: "符号结构不是由耦合强度决定，而由两条边在约束图里是并联还是串联（共享节点的相容/不相容）决定". Also gives the "collective snapping without external drive on the second unit" precedent, which directly parallels the recorded same-γ double flip.

Also, the shell cap "continuous route near threshold" supports my "third admissible state / 浮动" as a near-threshold phenomenon: near-threshold geometry gives continuous transitions; far below threshold → snap. So a rotor near the "R ≈ ℓ0" critical (over-center / zero-stiffness) would pass through a continuous branch instead of snapping — which is precisely my "吸附式双稳 vs 连续可逆"边界 and predicts that "浮动" is not a generic third state but a near-threshold continuous branch. That refines the third state: instead of a binary "float or not", the continuous branch exists in a band of parameters near the threshold (R−ℓ0 sign is only the sharp criterion in the small-deflection idealization; finite geometry smears it into a band). That's a correction: my hypothesis said "R<ℓ0 ⇒ cannot float; R>ℓ0 ⇒ floats", a sharp criterion; published near-threshold continuous transition suggests a band, so classification of a rotor as "constrained bistable" vs "continuous reversible" is not a parameter-free sharp cut; and closeness to threshold makes the observable amount of "silent" motion grow continuously.

That's a good learning_change: revise unilateral_stop_state's sharp sign criterion into a band, adding that near-threshold the transition is continuous, and that the "float" is a limit of the continuous branch, not a distinct state.

Also method K413da: bistability conditions depend on axial force level (two solution branches) — transfer: for the rotor-spring with installation offset, the analogue of "axial force level" is the spring pre-tension (ℓ0 relative to current R), i.e. the sign/magnitude of net spring tension, which is exactly the quantity I claimed decides stability. Published analysis shows the transition between solution branches is governed by the axial force level combined with initial shape amplitude — supports my "R−ℓ0" but shows that it is one of two parameters (initial shape amplitude x_offset and axial force), so "same geometry switching by changing ℓ0" is a special case of a two-parameter family. Good: this makes my claim concrete but corrects "one sign" to "a boundary in the (initial shape amplitude, axial load) plane".
